# Investigating Relaxation Phenomena in Vortex Matter Through Stimulated Dynamics

The mechanical method of investigating Abrikosov vortex stimulated dynamics was employed to study relaxation phenomena occurring within the vortex matter of high-temperature superconductors. This experimental approach enabled detailed observation of how vortex systems evolve and respond under controlled external perturbations, providing valuable insight into the fundamental behavior of these complex magnetic structures.

Through these investigations, pulsed magnetic fields were found to significantly alter the course of relaxation processes occurring within the vortex matter. The application of such pulses proved capable of modifying the natural progression of relaxation, demonstrating that external stimulation can directly influence the dynamic state of the vortex system.

Experiments conducted on isotropic HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋ᵈ superconductors revealed the existence of threshold phenomena. Specifically, short-duration pulses were observed to have no measurable effect on the relaxation processes, indicating that a minimum condition must be satisfied before the vortex matter responds to external stimulation. This threshold behavior points to a characteristic timescale governing the response of the vortex system.

When the pulse duration exceeded a critical threshold value, however, the relaxation process was found to change markedly. This transition was clearly evidenced by a stepwise shift in the relaxing mechanical moment, signaling a distinct alteration in the state of the vortex matter once the critical pulse duration had been surpassed.

On the basis of these observations, the formation time of the Abrikosov vortex lattice in HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋ᵈ was determined to be approximately 20 microseconds. Notably, this value exceeds by an order of magnitude the time required to form a single vortex in type II superconductors, highlighting the more complex and collective nature of vortex lattice formation as compared to the establishment of an individual vortex.

# Investigation of Relaxation Phenomena in the Vortex Matter of HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ

## Introduction

The dynamics of vortex matter in high-temperature superconductors remains one of the most intensively studied topics in condensed matter physics, owing to both its fundamental importance and its practical implications for technological applications. Understanding the mechanisms of flux penetration, vortex lattice formation, and the relaxation processes that govern the evolution of the vortex system is essential for controlling and optimizing superconducting materials. In this work, we employed the mechanical method of stimulated vortex dynamics to investigate relaxation phenomena in the vortex matter of the isotropic high-temperature superconductor HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ. Particular attention was devoted to examining how pulsed magnetic fields of varying durations and amplitudes influence these relaxation processes.

## Experimental Approach

The mechanical method of stimulated vortex dynamics provides a sensitive probe of the collective behavior of the vortex ensemble. In this technique, the superconducting sample is subjected to external magnetic field pulses, and the resulting mechanical response—expressed through changes in the mechanical moment acting on the sample—is monitored as a function of the pulse parameters. By systematically varying the duration and amplitude of the applied magnetic field pulses, it becomes possible to disentangle the characteristic timescales governing the rearrangement of the vortex configuration.

The choice of HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ as the material of study is motivated by its isotropic properties, which simplify the interpretation of the vortex dynamics by minimizing the complications arising from strong anisotropy present in many layered cuprate superconductors. This isotropy allows the intrinsic behavior of the vortex lattice to be examined more directly.

## Results and Discussion

The measurements revealed the existence of pronounced threshold phenomena in the relaxation behavior of the vortex matter. Specifically, magnetic field pulses whose duration exceeded a certain critical value were found to alter the relaxation process in a distinctly different manner than shorter pulses. This alteration manifested as stepwise, discrete changes in the mechanical moment of the sample, indicating that the vortex system underwent qualitative reorganization only when the applied stimulus persisted beyond the critical timescale.

The observation of such threshold behavior carries significant physical meaning. It implies that the formation and rearrangement of the Abrikosov vortex lattice is not an instantaneous process but rather requires a finite time for the coordinated establishment of the ordered flux-line configuration. When the pulse duration was shorter than this characteristic time, the vortex lattice could not fully form or reorganize, and the stepwise transitions in the mechanical moment were absent. Conversely, pulses longer than the threshold provided sufficient time for the collective vortex structure to develop, producing the observed discrete changes.

From the analysis of the critical pulse duration at which these stepwise changes emerged, the characteristic formation time of the Abrikosov vortex lattice was determined to be approximately 20 microseconds. This value is of particular interest when compared with theoretical estimates of the formation time of a single vortex in type II superconductors. The measured lattice formation time proved to be roughly an order of magnitude greater than that required for the nucleation of an individual vortex. This substantial difference underscores the fundamentally collective nature of vortex lattice formation: whereas a single vortex can nucleate relatively rapidly, the establishment of the fully ordered Abrikosov lattice involves the mutual interaction and coordinated arrangement of many vortices, a process that necessarily requires considerably more time.

## Conclusions

The application of the mechanical method of stimulated vortex dynamics to the isotropic high-temperature superconductor HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ has enabled a detailed examination of the relaxation phenomena in its vortex matter. The study established the existence of threshold phenomena governed by the duration of the applied magnetic field pulses, with pulses exceeding a critical duration inducing stepwise changes in the mechanical moment. Most importantly, these results allowed for the determination of the Abrikosov vortex lattice formation time as approximately 20 microseconds—an order of magnitude longer than the single-vortex formation time characteristic of type II superconductors. These findings provide valuable insight into the temporal aspects of collective vortex dynamics and contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying flux organization in high-temperature superconducting materials.

# Abrikosov and the Physics of Superconductivity

**The** name Alexei Abrikosov stands as one of the most influential figures in the field of condensed matter physics. Born in 1928 in the Soviet Union, Abrikosov dedicated his career to understanding the mysterious behavior of superconducting materials, ultimately earning the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2003.

**With** his groundbreaking theoretical work, Abrikosov transformed our understanding of how superconductors respond to magnetic fields. His most celebrated contribution came in 1957, when he predicted the existence of what would later be called the Abrikosov vortex lattice. This discovery revealed that certain superconductors—now classified as type-II superconductors—allow magnetic fields to penetrate through them in the form of tiny, quantized vortices arranged in a regular geometric pattern.

**The** significance of Abrikosov's work extends far beyond theoretical curiosity. His predictions about vortex behavior have practical implications for developing powerful superconducting magnets, which are essential components in technologies ranging from MRI machines to particle accelerators. Understanding how these vortices form, move, and interact allows engineers to design more efficient and stable superconducting systems.

**With** collaboration and continued research, the principles Abrikosov established have inspired generations of physicists. His theoretical framework, developed alongside contemporaries like Lev Landau and Vitaly Ginzburg, laid essential groundwork for modern quantum physics.

**The** legacy of Abrikosov reminds us that theoretical insights, though sometimes abstract, can unlock revolutionary technologies and deepen our comprehension of the natural world.

# Magnetic Relaxation Dynamics in Type II Superconductors Under Pulsed Fields

## Abstract

We report measurements of mechanical moment relaxation in type II superconductors subjected to controlled magnetic field pulses, with emphasis on determining the critical pulse duration governing flux penetration and the characteristic timescale for Abrikosov vortex lattice formation.

## Experimental Method

A type II superconducting sample was mounted on a torsional suspension to measure the mechanical moment induced by applied magnetic pulses. Field pulses of variable duration (τ_p) and amplitude were applied while the sample was maintained below its critical temperature (T_c). The mechanical response was recorded as a function of pulse parameters, allowing extraction of relaxation dynamics associated with magnetic flux redistribution within the specimen.

## Key Findings

**Critical Pulse Duration.** A threshold pulse duration (τ_c) was identified, below which the applied field fails to establish a stable vortex configuration. For τ_p < τ_c, the mechanical moment exhibited incomplete relaxation, indicating that flux lines do not fully penetrate the bulk. Above this threshold, the moment approached its equilibrium value characteristic of the mixed state.

**Vortex Formation Time.** The formation of Abrikosov vortices was found to proceed on a finite timescale (τ_v), reflecting the nucleation and ordering of quantized flux lines into a lattice. The measured relaxation of mechanical moment was consistent with an exponential approach to equilibrium, with the time constant governed by τ_v and by flux-pinning interactions.

**Relaxation Behavior.** The decay of the mechanical moment followed the expected logarithmic-to-exponential crossover associated with flux creep and thermally activated depinning, confirming that the observed mechanical signal directly tracks the internal magnetic state.

## Conclusions

The experiment establishes a direct correspondence between mechanical moment relaxation and internal vortex dynamics. The identification of a critical pulse duration and a finite vortex formation time provides quantitative insight into the transient response of type II superconductors and constrains models of flux penetration under non-equilibrium conditions.
